blocks.3: In addition to the kings who, according to history and legend, we believe were here in the saga age, we have also had royal visits later; compare the local history, volume I, p. 214.
blocks.4: The periodical “Vidar”, in the bound edition of 1889, describes Christian V's journey in Norway in 1685. Page 322 mentions the journey in our parts. The king and his retinue came from the north in the “winged boats of Bergenhus”; they dined here and in the afternoon travelled on southwards. This was on 2 July 1685. I have seen nothing about how many were in the king's retinue here, but many well-known men who travelled with him from Copenhagen are named, at least over 30.
blocks.5: According to “Norske Samlinger” by Christian C.A. Lange, vol. 2, p. 99, Gyldenløve was in “Evenvig” with “Hr. Truls” on 29 June 1695. The priest here at that time was called Truls Glad. According to the local history this was Ulrik Frederik Gyldenløve. He was not a king, but a son of Frederick III.
blocks.6: Frederick IV was here in 1704. This is described in “Illustreret Nyhedsblad” 1859, p. 155. The king stayed the night here from 14 to 15 July 1704.
blocks.7: I have seen nothing more about these royal visits. It was the priests who ran most things in the villages at that time, so it was probably at the parsonage that the royal guests were received and “looked after” with both food and lodging.
blocks.8: The royal visit closest to us, which some people still remember and which has the most lustre about it, is the visit the elected King Haakon VII made here on 27 May 1936. My information about this event comes from newspaper reports of the king's journey and from people who remembered this “great occasion”. Here I would particularly like to mention Ivar Henriksbø and Olav Undertun, who both had good memories and could tell many details of the visit.
blocks.9: This year the Norwegian Forestry Society held its annual meeting outside Oslo for the first time. The meeting was held in Bergen, and in connection with it a tour of the western counties was organised to look at the forests, especially the plantations in our villages. It was looked forward to with excitement, and there was great joy that King Haakon had let it be known that he was interested in joining the tour.
blocks.10: Wednesday 27 May 1936 began as an ordinary weekday in Eivindvik. There was a north wind and brilliant sunshine. People went about their usual work, busy with the spring farming. During the day word came that the king would visit the village, but shortly afterwards it was reported that the royal visit could not take place after all. But then, in the afternoon, a telephone call came from Bergen saying that King Haakon and his retinue were now leaving the city with the forestry society on Fylkesbaatane's flagship “Nordfjord I”, and that they had decided to visit Eivindvik.
blocks.11: The message went round and people quickly gathered for a few hectic hours of preparation. The steamer quay was decorated with birch branches and flags. Gradually a great many people gathered on the quay and in the area around it. Many small boats, decorated with leafy branches and flags, went out to meet the royal ship.
blocks.12: At about half past seven “Nordfjord I” pushed her bow past Tangen and swung into Prestesundet. On the rocks where Eivindvik Slipp og Mek. verkstad (the slipway and engineering works) is now, a group of men stood ready, with fuses, detonators and dynamite, to begin the royal salute. When the boat was level with Haukøya, the first shot rang out. The proud ship slowed and glided majestically and calmly in to the boom of the thundering salute. The firing went very well. The men standing there were precise with the fuses and steady of hand when lighting them, and did the job well without modern ignition equipment. Indeed, the 21 shots came so evenly that the king asked whether they had saluting cannons here. As the salute neared its end, the boat with the king and his retinue glided slowly past the rocks where the “saluters” stood. The king came over to the rail, the men ashore waved to the king and shouted “Hurrah” and “long live the king”, and King Haakon replied by taking off his hat and waving back.
blocks.13: As the boat approached the quay, the mood among the people rose, and the boat glided in to land to solemn singing from those gathered. “God bless our good king” rang out. Then came loud cheering and shouts of hurrah. The welcome was heartfelt. The king stood at the rail, and so many people streamed to that side of the boat that it listed heavily. Dean Hovden gave a solemn, warm and stirring speech of welcome, in which he welcomed the king to Gulen and to the site of the old Gulating. He opened by quoting some words Henrik Ibsen gave to one of the earls: “This is a great day for Norway!”
blocks.14: “When we here in this little village learned of this high visit a few hours ago”, he said, “these words came to my mind. A wave of pride runs through us. It is the great hour of our village. It is a long time since we have had a visit from the King of Norway here. We could have wished our mountains were more wooded than they are when the king visits us, but the sun gilds the mountains even though they are bare, and the sun gilds our hearts in warm thanks to His Majesty and the people of the forestry society.”
blocks.15: Afterwards the king thanked them warmly for the heartfelt welcome. He spoke from the ship's rail in humorous terms. He was impressed by how well and finely they had arranged everything in such a short time. The soil here must be very fertile, he said, since they had got the birch forest to grow so lushly on the quay in just a few hours. It had been said that it was a long time since any king had visited the place. He hoped that the King of Norway would always be just as welcome, and thanked them on his own and the forestry society's behalf for the heartfelt reception. Both speeches were greeted with great applause.
blocks.16: After his well-turned speech of thanks the king went ashore. He seemed to be in fine form, shook hands with people on the quay and chatted lively with those gathered. Hans Undertun stepped forward and thanked the king for the fine chandeliers Gulen church had received, which the king greatly appreciated. The two chandeliers are a personal gift from Queen Maud and King Haakon.
blocks.17: From the quay the party walked along the road towards Midtunvågen to look at the plantation at Midtun. This plantation is described as the oldest in Western Norway and at that time probably also the largest. When they looked in over the village, the king is said to have said: “This is a beautiful village.”
blocks.18: The party probably stopped at Stihaugen. From there they looked up at the plantation. “Forestry experts made many remarks about how impressed they were by what had been achieved here in almost treeless Gulen”, said a newspaper report of the tour. Because time was short, they turned at Stihaugen and walked out towards the area by the church where the stone crosses stand. Out by Borgstova, on the rock called Lovseieberget (the law-speaking rock), the head of national programming, Olav Midttun, gave a speech. A newspaper report says that Midttun, whose family came from Gulen, gave a speech that carried the whole gathering with him. He opened by saying that one condition for the assembly to be opened is that the king is present. He is the most important person at the assembly. Now the king has come and the assembly is in session.
blocks.19: His speech was steeped in history, and the speaker told of the old Gulating. Judging by the newspapers, he spoke in very well-chosen words that made a strong impression on both the king and the crowd. He spoke of the pioneer Dean Niels Griis Alstrup Dahl and quoted from Henrik Wergeland's poem “Eivindvig”. He said that the village here has also shown its faith in the future today through its pioneering work for forestry in Western Norway. He believed it was the planting here that prompted Noregs Ungdomslag (the national youth association) to take up the work of reforesting Western Norway. “The strongly personal speech, delivered at the historic place with Haakon VII as the natural centre, made an extraordinarily strong impression.” (From a newspaper report.) He ended his speech by giving the floor to the king.
blocks.20: King Haakon VII on the law-speaking rock at the Gulating site, Professor Olav Midttun on the far right. Photo: Unknown
blocks.21: A deeply solemn mood filled the moment. King Haakon had to take out his handkerchief to wipe his eyes. He again thanked them for the “heartfelt” way he had been received. He expressed great joy at being able to stand here at this place where the Gulating is thought to have been held. He found it a great thing that this should fall to him. The stalwart people's king was clearly moved.
blocks.22: The king and his retinue also went up to see St Olav's spring and the cross at Krossteigen. Then they went back to the quay and aboard “Nordfjord I” again. On departure the landowner Vilhelm Mohr thanked the villagers for the splendid reception. As “Nordfjord I” slid away from the quay, the people sang “Mellom bakkar og berg” (Among hills and rocks), and then came another salute, this time four powerful shots. The bangs rolled between the mountains and hung over the sound in the evening sun like a release of genuine joy at a successful royal visit and a great memory for the people of the village.
blocks.23: King Haakon is said to have later expressed that the visit here was a very rich experience for him too. For the village the visit will stand as a rich memory and as an example of how the improvised can often be very successful and leave the most lasting and best marks.
blocks.25: The royal yacht has anchored in Prestesundet in Eivindvik, and people are waiting for the King and Queen to come ashore at Prestebryggja. Photo: H.P. Martinussen.
blocks.26: At least as great were the joy and celebration when King Harald V and Queen Sonja visited the village in June 2002. This time the visit was planned, a great many people had turned out, and the mood was high when the royal yacht “Norge” anchored in the sound and the royal couple came ashore at Prestebryggja. They were received with flowers by 2 schoolchildren, Elise Midtun and Lars Tomas Unneland Larsen, by the mayor Trude Brosvik, the county governor, the county mayor and others.
blocks.27: During a tour of the village they showed great interest in the history connected with the place, and the queen in particular studied the stone crosses closely. Later they attended a performance of Håkonarspelet (the Håkon play) at Flolid, and in the evening there was a festive dinner with the municipal council and other invited guests at the community hall. Even though the rain was almost “bucketing” down, the event was a great success. The king said in a TV interview afterwards that “we got to experience Western Norway at its wettest, but the play itself was so interesting that we did not notice the rain”.
